# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why3: Any deaf or hard-of-hearing adult knows how much of last week's conversation they followed; it is their own lived experience.
screens.why4: The ladder is complete from all to nothing, but 'Caught only the gist' and 'Missed most of it' can both be true of the same dinner, since getting the gist often means missing most of the words.
screens.why5: My rungs are kept almost word for word, Kwame's 'nodding along at 20%' still lands on 'Missed most of it', and nothing about the glasses leaks.
screens.why7: Every rung is a step on how much of the talk was followed, best to worst. The first rung works and the last fails outright. The line sits under 'Missed only a little', so 1 to 2 rungs count against the belief and 3 to 5 count for it, and the bar names a rung that is on the list.
screens.instead: Keep the scale, but make rung 3 'Followed about half of it' so it doesn't overlap with 'Missed most of it'.

screens.why1: This is the reviewed Check after I saved how they deal with it today, so reading back the five outcomes and the line is exactly what comes next.
screens.why2: Followed everything, missed a little, caught the gist, missed a good part, couldn't follow at all is how my users and I talk about a table conversation.
screens.why3: Every deaf or hard-of-hearing adult knows from last week's dinner or meeting how much of it they actually followed.
screens.why4: 'Caught only the gist' and 'Missed a good part of it' overlap, since someone who got only the gist has also missed a good part, so a respondent could tick either.
screens.why5: My 'lost the thread and mostly nodded along' rung, softened earlier to 'Missed most of it', is now 'Missed a good part of it'; that blurs the nodding-along state my co-founder describes at 20% understanding.
screens.why7: All five rungs grade one measure, how much of the conversation was followed, from best to failing outright; two working rungs sit above the line under 'Missed only a little', three shortfalls sit below it, and the bar names a rung on the final list.
screens.instead: Followed everything that was said · Missed only a little · ┄ line ┄ · Caught only the gist · Missed most of it · Could not follow it at all

screens.why1: Choosing the interviewer belongs just before the link goes out, but a screen built around picking a voice is abrupt for a study whose respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing; it should start from how they will take in the questions.
screens.why2: Daphne, Saskia, the 5-second samples, 400 credits and the text-message link are all clear to me on first read.
screens.why3: I can pick an interviewer for my own study, though my co-founder with hearing loss couldn't judge the voice samples by ear.
screens.why4: Two voices are a fair choice, but for my people the option that matters is missing: a text-first or captioned interviewer, or an ASL signer, for the Deaf respondents who don't voice.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and shows nothing of AirCaps or the glasses to respondents.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults get your questions? Written on screen with a captioned video interviewer (Daphne / Saskia) · Written on screen only · Signed in ASL, with captions

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it's natural to choose the format, and for my users the format matters a lot.
screens.why2: Each option is described in plain words, so the name 'Daphne' doesn't trip me up and I can pick on first read.
screens.why3: I know my people: most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults would rather read and tap than follow a spoken interviewer, so this is mine to decide.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete, and the AI option notes that every question is also written on screen, which keeps it usable for a deaf respondent.
screens.why5: Nothing about caption glasses or my product leaks into the format choice, and my pick of 'Read and tap' is kept as I made it.

screens.why1: Once I've picked how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults will answer, the next step is deciding who gets the link, so it belongs at the end of the sending step.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and the Contacts page and Google sign-in are named right inside the options. The only wobble is that the second option switches from 'I' to 'you' mid-line.
screens.why3: I know who I'm sending to: the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already know from TranscribeGlass days and our testimonials.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link for a group (an HLAA chapter or a Deaf community forum) are distinct and cover how I'd actually reach people; no escape chip is needed for a choice of channel.
screens.why5: Nothing about AirCaps or the glasses leaks here, and my pick, people I know by name, is kept as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People I found with Keel (I pick a list from the Contacts page; Keel makes a link for each and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is up top with a number beside it, but the number is the median of 4 days, which sits inside my own 4-to-7 range and reads like a hold; the real deciding figure (4 of 7 at or beyond, bar 5, 1 short) is buried on the card, not beside the verdict.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives the count over 7 and its bar, but the Frequency card says the split twice in different forms and Importance repeats '7 of 7 put it in their two', so I had to reread to find which number meets which bar.
screens.why_b3: The four dimensions and belief lines are mine (8 in 10 lost the thread, 4 to 7 days, keeping the thread in their top two, today's way falls short), and the statement uses my table, background-noise and 20%-at-best words; only the Importance line is clunkily phrased.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what the Frequency split means for AirCaps, for example whether to aim at people who lose the thread 2 to 3 days a week or tighten the segment; the only closing text is a generic note on how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: The '7 people answered' count is visible throughout, but nothing says 7 is a small sample, and 'Holding up' on '8 in 10 of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults' from 7 people reads firmer than the data can carry.
screens.instead: Frequency fell one short: 4 of 7 lose the thread 4+ days a week, and you needed 5. The other 3 hit it 2 to 3 days, so either aim at the daily-group crowd or plan for part-week use. With 7 people, treat all four as early reads.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I see both that it held and why it held.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven cells all for me on a 0 to 7 axis, with the marker at 6 labelled as my bar, so the count, the people and the bar are clear at first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief drops my segment's qualifiers ('in the US who talk with hearing people every week'), and the Asked line carries a stray tail ('the most recent time it happened'), so it is recognisably mine but not exactly what I typed.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' points me onward, but it doesn't say what a held Prevalence means for the idea, such as that the wedge is real enough to keep testing frequency and cost.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says plainly 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so it makes no claim beyond these seven.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost the thread of a conversation in the last 7 days; all 7 said yes, a lean rather than a call, so the problem is common enough to check next whether it comes often and costs enough to pay for.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside "4 of 7 at or beyond what you said · bar 5 of 7 · 1 short", so I know it missed by one person and why, though the verdict line repeats the same split three ways.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7, 7 people and the bar at 5 of 7 are all there, but the legend's "what you said" next to "at what you said" took me a second look, and so did an axis starting at 0 when nobody could answer 0.
screens.why_b3: Frequency, my 4 to 7 days out of 7, and my deaf and hard-of-hearing adults losing the thread with hearing people: that is the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" only points me onward; it doesn't say what 3 of 7 losing the thread on fewer days means for an all-day glasses pitch built on 6+ hours of daily use.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the card calls it "a small group: a lean, not a call", though tagging a count-of-days question with "the most recent time it happened" muddles what was asked.
screens.instead: Drop "the most recent time it happened" from the asked line, and have the So line say: 3 of 7 lose the thread on only 1 to 3 days, so pitch the glasses for the week's hard conversations, not for all-day wear.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the strip with its marker at 5 are clear, but the caption says 'each picked two' while the bars add to 11, not 14, so I had to stop and work out that three people picked Nothing else.
screens.why_b3: Importance is the dimension I checked, and 'Keeping the thread of the conversation' is the hurt I named: losing the thread when the talk is too fast or noisy, with deaf and hard-of-hearing adults and my circumstance in my own words.
screens.why_b4: The So line explains what top-two means, but it never tells me what to do, such as building captions around following the thread first and treating getting a word in as a second need.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' warns me off over-reading 7 of 7, and the So line does not claim it ranks first.
screens.instead: Caption the chart '7 people · 11 picks (3 picked only this one)', and add a line like: all 7 put following the thread in their two, so lead with live captions for group talk; getting a word in (3) is the next need to watch.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The five rungs each carry a count and a for or against, the line is drawn under 'Missed only a little', and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against out of 7 with the marker at 5, all clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief and the bar line use my act and my rung words ('following what hearing people said', 'Missed only a little'), and that is the conversation-following I care about, even though 'join' fell out of the act.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' points forward but stays generic, and it doesn't say what the gap means for my glasses: three people got only the gist and three missed a good part, so captions have to lift people past the gist.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible everywhere, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' tempers a 6 of 7 result, and nobody is counted beyond those who answered.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7, and every shortfall is getting the gist or missing a good part, never losing it all. So the glasses have to get people from the gist to nearly everything, and that is what to test next.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', and the body repeats 'Current solution held, 6 of 7', so I know it held and by how much against the bar.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' is my dimension, but 'following what hearing people said still falls short' is Keel's rewording of my circumstance (too fast or too noisy to follow); I recognise it, but it isn't how I'd say it.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what the single holdout means for AirCaps (e.g. whether single-sided deafness is outside the wedge), and the 'When a line fails' header on a line that held points me nowhere.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and the single 'against' are visible, but the 'When a line fails' heading over a held line is a soft mislabel, and nothing notes that 7 people is a small base.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's 'deaf on one side, I take the end seat and keep everyone on my good side' names a seating workaround that keeps unilateral loss outside my pain point, which my belief never spelled out.
screens.instead: Held, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5; the one who copes is deaf on one side and manages with seating, so people with single-sided loss may sit outside the day-one wedge.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it plainly checks whether I'm the kind of person the study is about before asking anything else.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and everyone I know talk about it, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I'm talking with hearing people: at work, at the shops, with my family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a screener, and no escape is needed here.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's own line about talking with hearing people every week, and nothing about a product or a company's plan leaks to me.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and two options, and I'd catch it on one hearing or reading of the captions.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it's obvious why they'd ask whether I lost track of one of those conversations this week.
screens.why2: "Lose the thread" is exactly how I'd put it; I don't need to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know whether I got lost in a conversation with hearing people in the last seven days, because it's the thing I notice most.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and both are true for someone; the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, so they don't bother me here.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks to me, but "face-to-face" has gone, so a phone call or video chat I lost track of could slip in, and that's a different problem for me.
screens.why6: One short sentence ending "Yes or no" is easy to take in once, whether I read it on the screen or catch it aloud.
screens.why7: A two-answer gate with no escape that asks about the thing that goes wrong, not the routine: on a quiet one-to-one week I could truly say No, and on a week at a noisy dinner I'd say Yes.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose the thread of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to losing the thread this week, asking how many days it happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Lose the thread of a conversation with hearing people" is how I'd describe it myself, and counting days out of the last 7 is easy.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I sat at work or at dinner nodding along after I'd lost what people were saying, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button for each day from 1 to 7, no zero since I already said yes, and "I can't recall" fits for a week where the days blur together.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company comes through; it only asks about my conversations.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and "say a number from 1 to 7" is easy to answer by ear, or on the captions in my case.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the 7-day window, ordered 1 to 7, with no zero and no bands, and "I can't recall" is the only escape; the founder's range isn't shown, but these buttons can be split for or against any range that starts at 2 or higher.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which part of these talks I'd most want easier.
screens.why2: All three are things I'd say myself; 'keeping the thread' matches the 'lose the thread' wording from the screen before.
screens.why3: Each is something I've dealt with at a dinner or a meeting this week: jumping in before the topic moves on, keeping up, and needing a rest from lip-reading without walking off.
screens.why4: Three distinct, real difficulties in my words, none swallowing another, and 'None of these' covers me if it's something else, like asking people to repeat.
screens.why5: Nothing here hints at a product or a company's idea; it's just about the conversation.
screens.why6: Short stem, three short options read as a list I can hold, one escape at the end; easy to take in once (with captions on, for me).
screens.why7: The own row, keeping the thread, sits second among three with two other rows, so I could fill both picks without it; 'None of these' is offered at the first ask.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? (same three options, None of these)

screens.why1: After choosing what I'd most like made easier, asking how well I actually followed the last conversation is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but 'how did following what hearing people said go' is a clumsy phrase, and 'your last conversation' alone made me wonder for a second whether it meant one with Deaf friends too.
screens.why3: I know exactly how much I caught at my last chat with hearing people, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: The five cover it and the escape fits, but 'Caught only the gist' and 'Missed a good part of it' blur together, because catching only the gist usually means I missed a good part.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder leaks through, and 'hearing people' and 'follow' are words I'd use myself.
screens.why6: It is one question with five short options I can hold, but the stem 'how did following what hearing people said go' is a mouthful when heard once.
screens.why7: All five are steps on one measure (how much of what was said I followed), best to worst, with a working first rung, an outright failure last, and the single 'I can't recall' escape the card asks for on an act I can't hand off.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? All of it · Nearly all of it · About half of it · Only bits of it · None of it · or I can't recall
